[1] The spring I moved back into my parents' house, at twenty-three, with a degree and no job, Mrs. Ilse Varga next door fell on her back steps and broke her hip. She was eighty-one. She had been the town's weather observer for forty-four years, which meant that every morning at seven, in every kind of weather, she walked to the white slatted box in her side yard, read two thermometers and a rain gauge, wrote the numbers on a form, and telephoned them to a regional office two hundred miles away. From the hospital her daughter called my mother, and my mother, without consulting me, said that I had nothing but time.

[2] I went over the first morning expecting a lesson and got a clipboard. The instructions were written on an index card taped inside the lid of the box, in a hand that leaned hard to the right: read the high, read the low, read the gauge, reset, record, call. Mrs. Varga had added a final line, underlined twice, that said only "Write what you see." I remember thinking it a strange thing to have to tell anyone.

[3] For three weeks I did exactly what the card said and resented every minute of it. Seven o'clock is early when nothing is waiting for you afterward. I made the readings in my pajamas, phoned them in to a recording that never once said thank you, and went back to bed. I told my friends that I was reading thermometers for an old woman, in a voice meant to make clear that I knew how it sounded.

[4] Mrs. Varga came home in April with a walker and a view of her yard from the kitchen window, and on her first morning back she asked to see the forms. She went down my three weeks with one finger. She stopped at the ninth of April, where I had written a zero in the precipitation column.

[5] "It rained that night," she said.

[6] I told her it had barely rained: there had been a film of water in the bottom of the gauge, not enough to reach the first mark, and so the amount was nothing.

[7] "Then it's a trace," she said, and she wrote a small T over my zero, carefully, without crossing the zero out, so that both could be read. "Zero means it didn't rain. Trace means it did and there wasn't enough to measure. Those are two different mornings." She said it without any heat, the way she might have told me which drawer held the spoons. Then she found two more zeros of mine that should have been traces, corrected them the same way, and handed the clipboard back.

[8] I was annoyed for most of a day, and at dinner I said to my mother that only a person with too little to do could care about so small a distinction. My mother said that a farmer out on the county road had once told her he planted by those numbers, and that a man from the state university came every few summers to copy the old forms by hand. I had pictured the forms going into a drawer. I had not pictured anyone reading them.

[9] I kept going over after that, even when Mrs. Varga could manage the steps again, because by then it was the one fixed point in my day. Some mornings she came out and stood by the box in her housecoat while we read the instruments together; some mornings she only watched from the window. Once, in June, I overslept and reached the box at a quarter to nine, and I stood there with the pencil, knowing the low had come hours earlier and that I could guess it within a degree. She had seen me from the kitchen. She did not come out. When I brought the form in, I had written "late, 8:45" across the top and left the low blank, and she read it and nodded and said nothing, which I understood was the most she would ever say.

[10] That fall I found a job two towns over, and the station passed to a retired mail carrier from across the street. Before I left I asked Mrs. Varga, a little grandly, whether she thought I had been any good at it. She considered it longer than I wanted her to. Then she said that I had been very good after April, and I realized she was not talking about the thermometers. I think about the T she wrote above my zero more often than makes sense. There have been whole seasons of my life since then that I was tempted to enter as nothing, and I have learned to look again, closer, at the bottom of the glass.

passage:
[1] By most counts, the United States has lost well over a quarter of its newspapers since the mid-2000s, and the large majority of the closures have been small weeklies rather than big-city dailies. The usual explanation is a single word: the internet. That explanation is true as far as it goes, but it does not go very far in a small town. The internet arrived everywhere at roughly the same time. The papers did not close everywhere at the same time, and many of them did not close at all.

[2] To see the puzzle, picture two county seats of about six thousand people each, a few hours apart, with similar incomes and similar main streets. Call them Arden and Colby; they are composites, not real places. In 2005 each had a weekly paper founded in the nineteenth century. Today Arden's still comes out every Wednesday. Colby's printed its last edition years ago, and residents now learn about their school board, if they learn about it at all, from a social media group run by a volunteer.

[3] The first explanation people reach for is that Arden must be richer or bigger. At the extremes, that is fair: the poorest and most isolated counties have lost papers at especially high rates. Across the broad middle, though, size and income sort the survivors from the casualties surprisingly poorly. Arden and Colby are not unusual in being alike on paper and different in outcome.

[4] A more useful question is where each paper's money came from. For decades, many papers depended heavily on classified advertising, the small paid listings for used cars, apartments, and jobs. When free listing websites appeared, that income collapsed quickly, and papers that leaned on it hardest felt the blow first. Many small weeklies had depended on classifieds less than papers in larger markets had, so the loss, while real, was smaller for them.

[5] Ownership mattered more. During the 2000s and 2010s, chains bought up hundreds of small papers, some of them backed by investment firms that expected steady returns. A common pattern followed: design, printing, and sometimes editing were moved to a regional office, and local reporting positions were cut to one or none. The paper kept its old name on the front page, but readers noticed that it no longer covered their town in particular. Subscriptions fell, and the falling subscriptions were then offered as proof that the town no longer wanted a paper. A locally owned weekly, whose owner lived down the street from the people being covered, was far less likely to make that trade, partly from loyalty and partly because the owner had no regional office to send the work to.

[6] The survivors also tended to cover what nobody else would. A city television station will not send a crew to a county commission meeting about a culvert, and a national website will not run the obituary of a retired school custodian. The papers that lasted kept doing those unglamorous things. Many of them were also helped by public notices: laws in most states require local governments to publish certain budgets, hearings, and sales in a newspaper, and the fees are a modest but dependable source of income. Several states have moved to let governments post such notices online instead, and small publishers watch those debates closely.

[7] Finally, the survivors were small on purpose. A typical one is run by an editor, a part-time reporter, and an owner who also sells the ads. It stopped trying, long ago, to be a miniature version of a city daily, and its costs are low enough that a few hundred subscribers and the local hardware store can keep it alive.

[8] None of this means that a well-run paper was safe. Some of the closures were of papers that had done everything right, and closed anyway when an owner retired and no buyer could be found. Stories about survival are always told from the survivors' side, and it is easy to mistake luck for strategy when looking back.

[9] Still, the pattern points somewhere. In the towns where papers lasted, the internet took something from them but did not decide their fate. What decided it, more often, was whether the paper remained something only it could provide, and whether someone nearby was willing to keep providing it.

Passage A

[1] I have spent much of my working life preparing books that their authors did not finish. People sometimes ask whether I feel like a trespasser, and the honest answer is that I did at first. A manuscript left in a desk drawer seems to carry its author's silence with it, and opening it feels like overruling that silence.

[2] The feeling fades once you have done the work. Every reader of modern fiction has heard that Franz Kafka asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts, and that Brod refused and published them instead, among them The Trial and The Castle. The case is usually told as a betrayal that happened to turn out well. I think that misdescribes it. A writer's wishes about his own pages are one interest among several, not a command that cancels the rest. Readers have an interest, and so does a literature that would be poorer without those books.

[3] Nor is an unfinished book the same as a bad one. Most drafts I have worked on are uneven, but the unevenness is itself instructive: a reader can see where the writer was sure and where he was still feeling his way. My job is to make that visible, not to hide it. I mark every place where the text breaks off, I print the alternate versions of a passage side by side, and I say plainly in the introduction what the author left undecided. A reader who meets the draft on those terms is not deceived about what he is holding.

[4] There is a further benefit that is rarely mentioned. Young writers learn more from a great writer's false starts than from his finished pages, because the finished pages hide the labor that produced them. I have had letters from students who said that seeing a master cross out his own sentences was the first time they believed that they could write at all.

[5] The alternative is to let the pages sit in an archive that a few specialists will visit. That protects the author's privacy, but it also turns a public loss into a private one.

Passage B

[6] I am a novelist, and I have left written instructions that none of my drafts is ever to be published as a book. I would like to explain why, because the request is usually taken for vanity, and it is closer to the opposite. A vain writer wants to be read as much as possible. I want to be read only for what I actually did.

[7] A draft is not a weaker copy of a finished book. It is a record of decisions not yet made. When I look at an early version of a chapter, I see sentences I kept only because I had not yet found the better ones, a character I was about to cut, and an ending I had already decided against but had not yet deleted. Published, that page tells a reader that I chose those things. I did not choose them. I simply had not finished choosing.

[8] Careful editors know this, and the best of them print every variant and flag every gap. I am grateful to them. But a book with my name on the cover will be read as a book, whatever the introduction says, and reviewers will quote its weakest sentences as evidence of what I thought good writing was.

[9] Kafka is always offered as the answer to writers like me, and I understand why. But he is remembered precisely because his case is rare. Nobody keeps a list of the drafts that were published against their authors' wishes and added nothing except embarrassment. If an argument rests on its single best example, it is worth asking what the other examples look like.

[10] I do not ask that the drafts vanish from history. Let them go to a library where a scholar who wants to study how a book was made can read them as working papers. What I object to is the bookstore, where a reader looking for a novel will be sold a desk drawer.

[1] For most of a typical year, the low deserts of the American Southwest look as if nothing in them is alive except the shrubs. Then, in some springs, the ground between the shrubs turns yellow and purple for a few weeks, and visitors drive hundreds of miles to see it. It is tempting to describe such a bloom as the desert's response to rain. That description leaves out the most interesting part. The rain is a signal, and the plants have to decide whether to believe it.

[2] The decision is hardest for the annuals, the small plants that sprout, flower, set seed, and die within a single season. An annual spends most of its existence as a seed lying in the soil, and it gets only one chance to grow. If it germinates after a light shower, the seedling will put out a root and a pair of leaves, the soil will dry within days, and the plant will die without ever flowering. For a desert annual, sprouting at the wrong time is not a small mistake. It is the end.

[3] Many desert annuals therefore do not sprout after just any rain. In experiments beginning in the mid-twentieth century, the botanist Frits Went and his colleagues found that seeds of several species stayed dormant after a light sprinkling but germinated after a soaking one. One explanation Went proposed was that the seed coats contain chemicals that block germination, and that only a heavy rain washes enough of them away. Temperature acts as a second filter. Species that grow through the cool months tend to germinate only when the soil is cool, so a warm summer thunderstorm, however heavy, leaves them in the ground.

[4] Even a soaking rain can mislead. A single storm may be followed by months of dry weather, and seedlings that trusted it will die. Desert annuals hedge against that risk in a way that resembles a cautious investor. In any given year, only a fraction of the seeds in the soil germinate, even when conditions look good; the rest stay dormant and wait for a later year. Long-term studies of desert plots have found seed banks in which some seeds remain viable for many years. A bad year can kill every plant that sprouted and still leave the population intact underground.
